# Exact obstructions to shared-integer fiber-power amplification

The purpose of this note is to audit a specific amplification mechanism. It
does not rule out every conceivable use of products or tilts.

## 1. The natural construction preserves the integer Helly factor

For a convex body C in R^n x R^d, define

`C^[k]={(z,x_1,...,x_k):(z,x_j) in C for every j}`.

It is a convex body in R^n x R^(kd): convexity follows by intersecting linear
preimages of C; boundedness is immediate; an interior point of C, repeated in
all continuous coordinates, gives an interior point. Its integer fiber at z
is `K_z^k`, of volume `v_z^k`, where `v_z=vol_d(K_z)`.

The usual mixed Helly centerpoint bound gives a point of its mixed-integer
set of depth at least `1/[2^n(kd+1)]`. Averaging its continuous coordinates
projects to a point of the ORIGINAL fiber K_z, so the membership requirement
is satisfied exactly.

The problem is that this projection need not have the desired original
halfspace depth. In fact the following example defeats EVERY Helly center
of these powers, for all sufficiently large k.

## 2. Explicit convex polygon

Let

`C=conv{(0,0),(3,0),(3,3),(2,10),(0,2)}` in R x R.

Its integer fibers are the intervals

`I_0=[0,2]`, `I_1=[0,6]`, `I_2=[0,10]`, `I_3=[0,3]`.

Their lengths are `(2,6,10,3)` and total mixed volume is 21. Their midpoints
are `(z,m_z)` with `m=(1,3,5,3/2)`.

Every midpoint has original depth strictly below 1/4. Certified containing
halfspaces and their unnormalized mixed masses are:

* z=0: `x>=11z+1`, mass 1;
* z=1: `x>=11(z-1)+3`, mass 5;
* z=2: `x>=9-2z`, mass 5;
* z=3: `x>=-11(z-3)+3/2`, mass 3/2.

Moreover, every point `(z,x)` with `|x-m_z|<1/8` still has depth below 1/4.
Shift the corresponding listed threshold by `x-m_z`. For z=0,1,3 the cap
mass changes by at most this absolute amount in this neighborhood. For z=2,
writing delta=x-5, the mass is `5-delta` if delta>=0 and `5-2delta` if
delta<=0. In every case the resulting mass is strictly below 21/4.

## 3. All powered Helly centers have bad average projections

Let Y_k be ANY point of `C^[k]` with normalized halfspace depth at least
`beta_k=1/[2(k+1)]`, and write its continuous-coordinate average as xbar_k.

For all sufficiently large k its integer coordinate must be 2. Indeed, a
vertical halfspace containing any other integer fiber and excluding fiber 2
has powered mass at most

`(2^k+6^k+3^k)/(10^k+6^k+3^k+2^k) <= 3(3/5)^k`,

which is eventually smaller than beta_k.

Conditional on fiber 2, the continuous coordinates are independent uniforms
on [0,10]. For their average Xbar and every delta>0,

`P(Xbar>=5+delta) <= exp(-k delta^2/50)`,
`P(Xbar<=5-delta) <= exp(-k delta^2/50)`.

For completeness, if U is uniform on [0,10], convexity of the exponential
and E(U-5)=0 give
`E exp(s(U-5))<=cosh(5s)<=exp(25s^2/2)`.
The last inequality follows by integrating `tanh t<=t`. Independence and
Markov's inequality, optimized at s=delta/25, give the displayed bounds.

If `|xbar_k-5|>=delta`, the corresponding average-coordinate halfspace
through Y_k therefore has powered mass at most

`exp(-k delta^2/50)+3(3/5)^k`.

This is eventually smaller than beta_k. Hence `xbar_k -> 5`, uniformly over
all eligible choices Y_k. Taking delta=1/8, Section 2 proves that the average
projection of EVERY such center eventually fails the original OC constant
1/4.

Thus applying the Helly bound to these shared-integer powers and projecting
by coordinate average cannot amplify the bound to OC, even in n=d=1.

The symmetry of the powered body and measure also allows any center to be
averaged over coordinate permutations, without decreasing its depth. The
resulting diagonal center has all coordinates equal to xbar_k. Accordingly,
selecting a coordinate from a symmetrized Helly center has the same failure.

## 4. Arbitrary exponential balancing of integer fiber weights does not repair it

The same conclusion holds if the powered measure is reweighted by
`exp(a_k z)` for ANY sequence of real tilts a_k. Conditional laws within each
fiber remain independent uniforms; only the fiber weights become

`exp(k log(l_z)+a_k z)`.

To prove the assertion, take any subsequence of k and pass further so that
`a_k/k` converges in the extended real line. If its limit is finite b, the
maximizers of `log(l_z)+bz` consist of either one integer or two ADJACENT
integers. This follows from strict discrete concavity:

`6^2>2*10`, `10^2>6*3`.

All other indices have a fixed positive limiting exponent gap and therefore
exponentially small total weight. If the limit is positive or negative
infinity, the unique dominant index is respectively 3 or 0, with the same
conclusion.

Let J be the resulting singleton or adjacent pair and let P be the segment
joining the original midpoint points `(z,m_z)` for z in J (a singleton is
allowed). Consider the pushforward of the tilted powered measure under
`(z,x_1,...,x_k)->(z,(sum x_j)/k)`.

If the projected center stays a fixed positive distance delta from P, a
separating line through it excludes the delta/2-neighborhood of P. On each
fiber in J, the exponential concentration bound above, applied to the
continuous coefficient of its unit normal, bounds the cap mass exponentially
in k. Fibers outside J also have exponentially small weight. This
contradicts the polynomial lower bound beta_k. Therefore the projected
center approaches P.

Its integer coordinate belongs to {0,1,2,3}. Since the endpoints of P have
adjacent integer coordinates, approaching P forces the point to approach one
of those endpoint midpoint points. Section 2 again gives a neighborhood on
which every original depth is below 1/4. Every subsequence admits such a
further subsequence, proving that for ANY tilt sequence and ANY sequence of
eligible Helly centers, their mean projections eventually fail 1/4.

This statement concerns linear exponential tilts of the INTEGER coordinate.
It does not claim to exclude arbitrary tilts of the continuous coordinates,
which change the conditional distributions and require a separate mass-loss
argument when transferring conclusions back to the original uniform measure.

## 5. Exact obstruction to independent auxiliary-fiber volume correction

A common proposed repair is to multiply the k-th power of each fiber by an
auxiliary convex fiber Q_z so that total fiber weight returns from `v_z^k`
to `v_z`. This requires

`vol_r(Q_z)=v_z^(1-k)`.

Already the concave interval-length profile `(v_0,v_1,v_2)=(1,2,1)` makes
this impossible for every k>1 and every positive auxiliary dimension r.
Convexity of the auxiliary family would imply

`(Q_0+Q_2)/2 subset Q_1`.

Brunn-Minkowski then gives

`vol_r(Q_1)^(1/r) >= (vol_r(Q_0)^(1/r)+vol_r(Q_2)^(1/r))/2 =1`,

whereas the required middle value is `2^((1-k)/r)<1`.

Even adding an arbitrary integer exponential tilt to the correction does not
help. Required volumes proportional to `exp(a z)v_z^(1-k)` would give

`exp(a/r)2^((1-k)/r) < exp(a/r)
                       <= (1+exp(2a/r))/2`,

again contradicting Brunn-Minkowski. This excludes the independent convex
auxiliary-fiber normalization construction, not more general couplings.

## 6. Two further exact pitfalls

A fiberwise join does not generally remain convex. For
`C={(z,x):1<=z<=3, 0<=x<=z}`, the proposed twofold fiberwise join consists of
`(z,u,xi_1,xi_2)` with `0<=u<=1`,
`0<=xi_1<=u z`, `0<=xi_2<=(1-u)z`.
It contains `(1,0,0,1)` and `(3,1,3,0)`, but their midpoint
`(2,1/2,3/2,1/2)` violates `xi_1<=u z=1`. Thus using a join to distribute
continuous dimensions while retaining one common integer coordinate requires
a new convexity argument; the naive construction is not convex.

Finally, the event that every coordinate lies in a cap is not an ambient
halfspace event on the power. For independent uniforms X_j on [0,1],

`P(X_j>=1/2 for every j)=2^(-k)`,

whereas the genuine average-coordinate halfspace has

`P((sum X_j)/k>=1/2)=1/2`.

The all-coordinates event is contained in the average halfspace, which is the
wrong inclusion for extracting a lower bound on the original cap probability
by taking a k-th root of a Helly lower bound. This issue is independent of
integer-factor growth.
